passage:
Monday.
Miss gave us the solar system model project, due Friday. Dilnaz from next door started hers the same evening. I told her mine would take ten minutes, because I'm Pranav, the fastest boy in class. I'll do it Thursday night.
Thursday night.
It is 10:30 and I am still painting Saturn. The thermocol balls took forever to cut. The paint won't dry. Jupiter fell off the stick twice. Ammi is helping with the hair dryer and she is not happy. I forgot that last time, the volcano project, I also started late and cried at midnight.
Friday.
It was finished at 6 a.m. Saturn's rings are sticky. Dilnaz's model had moons.

qa.q: How many times did Jupiter fall off the stick?
qa.a: Jupiter fell off the stick twice.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling on Thursday night at 10:30?
qa.a: He felt stressed and a bit panicky, still painting Saturn long after he thought he'd be done.

qa.q: What could Pranav do for the next project?
qa.a: He could remember how long the volcano project really took and start the same evening, like Dilnaz, instead of planning for ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel helping with the hair dryer late at night?
qa.a: Ammi is probably tired and annoyed, because the late start turned into her problem too.

grounding: A child's diary shows him expecting a project to take ten minutes, starting the night before and forgetting his past delays.

passage: In Ghoti village, Class 5 had to make a leaf book: twenty different leaves, pressed and labelled. It was due on Monday. "It'll take me ten minutes," Vijay told his sister Tanuja on Friday. "The leaves are right there, on the trees." Tanuja reminded him of the seed chart he'd rushed last term. "That was different," Vijay said. On Sunday afternoon he went out to collect. Some leaves were too high. The tamarind leaves were too small to label. The neem ones curled up in the heat. By sunset he had eleven. He went to bed with the book half empty, his stomach in a knot. Tanuja slipped a torch under his pillow in case he wanted to try the mango tree at dawn.

qa.q: How many leaves did Vijay have by sunset on Sunday?
qa.a: By sunset he had eleven.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he went to bed on Sunday?
qa.a: He felt anxious, his stomach in a knot, because the leaf book was only half done after he'd expected ten minutes.

qa.q: What would you advise Vijay for his next project?
qa.a: Remember how long the seed chart really took and start on the day the project is given, not the day before it is due.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Vijay's plan?
qa.a: Tanuja remembers his rushed seed chart, so she seems doubtful but kind, helping with a torch for dawn.

grounding: Shows a village child expecting a leaf project to take ten minutes, forgetting past rushes and running short of time.

passage: Emil had a poster on volcanoes due Wednesday at his school in Stockholm. On Monday, Soo-ah asked if he wanted to work in the library after class. "No need," Emil said. "It's one poster. Ten minutes." He pictured it: print three photos, write a title, done. On Tuesday evening he sat down at the kitchen table. The printer was out of ink. His mother drove him to the shop in the snow. The facts he'd found didn't fit on the paper, so he rewrote them twice. At nine his father found him in tears over a glue stick that had dried out. Emil remembered, too late, the same thing had happened with the Viking poster in autumn. Soo-ah's poster, finished on Monday, had a paper volcano that popped out.

qa.q: What was the printer out of on Tuesday evening?
qa.a: The printer was out of ink.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling at nine o'clock?
qa.a: He was upset and overwhelmed, in tears over a dried-out glue stick after expecting the poster to take ten minutes.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Emil pictured only the ideal path and forgot the Viking poster; next time he could plan for things going wrong and start on Monday like Soo-ah.

qa.q: How might Emil's parents feel about Tuesday evening?
qa.a: They were probably tired and a little frustrated, with a drive in the snow and a crying child late at night.

grounding: Shows a child imagining a poster will take ten minutes, starting the night before and forgetting a similar delay in the past.

passage:
Dear Vijay bhaiya,
You asked how the weekend of studying went. Honestly? It was a disaster.
On Friday I made a beautiful timetable: all eleven chapters of biology on Saturday and Sunday. Four hours per chapter, easy. I even colour-coded it.
By Saturday lunch I was still on chapter one. The diagrams took forever. By Sunday evening I had done three chapters, and I sat on the floor and cried. I was so shocked. Then Mummy, very quietly, reminded me that before the half-yearly I had planned the same thing for physics and managed four chapters.
So now I have nine days and eight chapters, and a new rule: I look at how long it actually took last time before I make a timetable.
Missing you,
Simran

qa.q: How many chapters of biology had Simran done by Sunday evening?
qa.a: Three chapters.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Simran felt shocked and overwhelmed, sitting on the floor crying because the weekend plan had fallen apart.

qa.q: What is Simran's new rule, and why does it help?
qa.a: To check how long a task actually took last time before making a timetable, so plans are built on real experience instead of hope.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt reminding Simran about the physics plan?
qa.a: Mummy probably felt sympathetic but wanted Simran to notice the pattern, so she said it very quietly.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows Simran planning to cover a whole syllabus in a weekend, ignoring past experience, and being shocked when it takes far longer.

passage: Hrithik, you have to hear this, because you'll do the same thing, I know you. So, I'm Asif, right, and on Friday I told everyone I'd finish the whole history syllabus over the long weekend. Three days, fourteen chapters. I had it all planned. Saturday: ancient. Sunday: medieval. Monday: modern plus revision. I even told my father to take the TV remote away. Saturday I did one and a half chapters. The Mauryan dates just would not stay in my head. Sunday there was a family lunch I'd completely forgotten. Monday I woke up at ten. I'd done four chapters. Four! And I was genuinely shocked, like somebody had stolen my time. But here's the thing: before the unit test I also planned five chapters a day, and I also did one. I just forgot.

qa.a: Four chapters.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling on seeing only four chapters done?
qa.a: Asif felt genuinely shocked and cheated, "like somebody had stolen my time," because the plan had seemed so realistic.

qa.q: What could Asif do before planning the next revision weekend?
qa.a: Look at how many chapters Asif really managed before the unit test and plan from that, leaving room for things like family lunches.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik react differently to Asif's plan on hearing it on Friday?
qa.a: Hrithik knows Asif well, so Hrithik might have doubted the fourteen-chapter plan from the start.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend about planning a whole syllabus in a long weekend, ignoring past records, and being shocked at how little got done.

passage:
Saturday morning, week 1. Vikas stuck a chart on his wall: the entire chemistry syllabus, all sixteen chapters, done this weekend. "Easy," he told his younger brother Yogesh. "Two days, eight chapters each." Yogesh, who remembered the maths weekend, said nothing.
Sunday night. Vikas had finished three chapters. Organic reactions alone had eaten the whole afternoon. He stared at the chart, face hot, and ripped it down. "How is that even possible?" he asked the ceiling.
Wednesday, week 2. Yogesh found a new chart on the wall, smaller. It said: "Real speed: about 1.5 chapters a day. Exam in 10 days. Plan: 1 a day plus 3 buffer days." Under it, in pen: "Stop planning like a hero." Vikas was at his desk, on chapter six.

qa.q: How many chapters had Vikas finished by Sunday night?
qa.a: Vikas had finished three chapters.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he ripped the chart down?
qa.a: He felt shocked and frustrated, his face hot, because the weekend plan had seemed so simple.

qa.q: What made Vikas's new chart better than the first?
qa.a: It was based on his real speed of about 1.5 chapters a day and added buffer days, instead of a hopeful picture.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt watching the first plan fall apart?
qa.a: Yogesh probably felt unsurprised and a bit sorry for his brother, since he remembered the maths weekend.

grounding: Shows over two weeks a teenager planning a whole syllabus in one weekend, being shocked when it takes much longer, and replanning from real speed.

passage: In Lunglei, Lalremsiami had three weeks left before her master's thesis was due at the college. Most of it was written, she told her friend Varun on the phone. "Just the field data from two villages. A week, maximum." Varun, who was writing his own thesis in Pune, asked how long the first village had taken. "That was the rainy season. This will be faster." But the bus to the second village ran only on alternate days. The headman was away at a wedding. Three families she needed to interview had gone to their jhum fields. By the last week she had half her data, and she couldn't sleep. She sat at her kitchen table at 2 a.m. writing an email to her guide asking for an extension, her hands cold. Varun called the next morning. "I'm asking for one too," he said.

qa.q: How often did the bus to the second village run?
qa.a: The bus ran only on alternate days.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling at 2 a.m. writing to her guide?
qa.a: She felt panicked and ashamed, sleepless with her hands cold, because the week she had planned had become three.

qa.q: What would have helped Lalremsiami plan better?
qa.a: Using how long the first village actually took, plus a buffer for buses and absent families, instead of a best-case week.

qa.q: How might Varun's call have felt to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: It probably felt comforting, since it showed she wasn't the only one who had underestimated a thesis.

grounding: Shows a student underestimating the time needed for thesis fieldwork and panicking as the deadline nears.

passage: Kwame had the scholarship portal open in his room in Accra and a whole week before the deadline. "Five applications, one a day," he told his flatmate Bao. "They're mostly the same essay." Bao, who had applied last year, raised an eyebrow. On Monday Kwame found the first one wanted two referees, not one. On Tuesday the second asked for a certified transcript, and the university office said three working days. The third essay prompt was completely different. By Friday night he had submitted one. He sat on his bed, laptop hot on his knees, heart racing, the deadline at noon the next day. Bao brought him tea and a printed checklist: "Every item for every form. Then decide which two you can really finish." Kwame took it and nodded, too tired to argue.

qa.q: How many applications had Kwame submitted by Friday night?
qa.a: He had submitted one.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling on Friday night?
qa.a: He felt panicked, heart racing, with the deadline at noon and only one of five applications done.

qa.q: What did Bao's checklist help Kwame do?

qa.q: How does Bao see Kwame's plan on Monday?

grounding: Shows a student expecting scholarship applications to be quick, meeting hidden steps and panicking near the deadline.

passage: The block office in Sindhudurg wanted a date. "When will the new toilet block at the Kudal school be ready?" the officer asked Pallavi. Everyone else had promised dates off the top of their heads. Pallavi, two years into her job as junior engineer, asked for a day. That evening she pulled out the files for the last three school toilet blocks in the taluka. The plan had said six weeks each time. They had taken nine, eleven and ten. Monsoon delays, a late cement lorry, a mason who fell sick. She broke the new job into parts on a sheet: foundation, walls, plumbing, tiling, inspection, and wrote a real range for each, with the old files beside her. Next morning she told the officer, "Ten weeks, and I'll update you at the end of each part." Her assistant Pooja whispered, "He won't like that." He didn't. But in week ten, the block opened.

qa.q: How long had the last three school toilet blocks actually taken?
qa.a: They had taken nine, eleven and ten weeks.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have felt when the officer asked for a date?
qa.a: She seemed calm but careful, not wanting to promise a number off the top of her head the way everyone else had.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Checking how long the past three blocks took, breaking the job into parts and giving a ten-week estimate, which proved accurate.

qa.q: How might the officer see Pallavi's ten-week answer at first?
qa.a: The officer probably felt impatient or annoyed, as Pooja predicted, since others promised quicker dates.

grounding: Shows a young engineer checking how long similar jobs really took, breaking the work into parts and adding a buffer before promising a date.

passage: The client in Busan wanted the game script translated by Friday. It was Monday. Soo-ah's first instinct was to say yes; it looked like a light job. Instead she opened the spreadsheet she'd kept since she started freelancing: every past job, the estimate she had given, and how long it actually took. Game scripts were always the trap. Her estimates had been two days; reality had averaged four, because of slang, jokes and the character names that needed notes. She split the new script into chunks: dialogue, menus, item descriptions, a final read. She put her real average next to each chunk and added a day for questions. Then she wrote to the client: "The following Tuesday, with a first half on Friday." Wei, the project manager, replied within minutes: "Tuesday works. Thanks for being straight with us."

qa.q: What had Soo-ah's past game-script jobs averaged in reality?
qa.a: Reality had averaged four days, though her estimates had been two.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah tempted to do first, and why did she resist?
qa.a: She felt tempted to say yes because it looked light, but she was wary, knowing game scripts were always the trap for her estimates.

qa.q: What small steps made Soo-ah's promise reliable?
qa.a: Checking her record of past jobs, splitting the script into chunks with real averages, and adding a day for questions.

qa.q: How does Wei seem to feel about the Tuesday date?
qa.a: Wei seems relieved and appreciative, thanking Soo-ah for being straight rather than promising Friday and missing it.

grounding: Shows a freelancer checking how long similar jobs really took, breaking the work into parts and adding a buffer before promising a date.

passage: The school library had to be fully digitised before the inspection, and the principal asked Sonali, the new librarian, for a finish date at the staff meeting. Tenzin, the computer teacher, said, "Two weeks, surely? It's just scanning barcodes." Sonali said she would answer on Monday. Over the weekend she looked at the logbook from the pilot she had run in the spring: one shelf of 200 books had taken four hours, not the two she had guessed, because half the barcodes were faded and had to be reprinted. The library had forty shelves. She split the job: reprinting labels, scanning, checking, and a week for damaged books. On Monday she said, "Seven weeks, and I'll tell you each Friday where we are." The principal frowned. Tenzin laughed. Seven weeks later, the last shelf went green on the screen.

qa.q: How long had one shelf of 200 books taken in the spring pilot?
qa.a: Four hours, not the two she had guessed.

qa.q: What might Sonali have been feeling when the principal frowned?
qa.a: She was probably a little uneasy but steady, confident her seven-week estimate was based on real evidence.

qa.q: What would you advise someone asked for a quick date at a staff meeting?
qa.a: Ask for time, check how long a similar piece of work really took, split the job into parts, and add a buffer, as Sonali did.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see the job at first?
qa.a: Tenzin sees it as simple barcode scanning that should take two weeks, not knowing about the faded labels.

grounding: Shows a new librarian using a past pilot to see how long the work really takes, breaking it down and adding a buffer before promising a date.

passage:
Sprint review, Friday. Notes for my own file.
Anirban said on Monday that the payment screen would be done by Wednesday. It was done this morning. Last sprint he said two days for the login fix; it took five. The others are similar. I've looked back at six sprints: almost every estimate from the team is short by about half.
It would be easy to call it laziness. I don't think it is. They work late. They're not lying. They're picturing the version where nothing goes wrong, which is what people do.
So from next week: I'll ask everyone for a range, "best case and likely case," not one date. And every Friday we'll look at last week's estimates next to what really happened, with no blame, just numbers.
Noor

qa.q: By about how much are the team's estimates short, according to Noor?
qa.a: Almost every estimate is short by about half.

qa.q: What does Noor feel about the team's missed dates?
qa.a: Noor feels understanding rather than annoyed, seeing the misses as a normal pattern of picturing the best case, not laziness.

qa.q: What is Noor's plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking for a best-case and likely-case range and reviewing estimates against reality every Friday without blame, so the team can learn their real speed.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel in the first Friday review?
qa.a: Anirban might feel nervous at first, then relieved to find the review is about numbers, not blame.

grounding: A team lead's note shows noticing teammates' repeatedly optimistic dates, treating it as a thinking pattern rather than laziness, and asking for ranges.

passage:
Wednesday night.
Eshaan told the client "next Monday" again today. Third time in a month he's promised a Monday, and third time it'll be Thursday. My first feeling was anger, honestly. I'm the one who calls the client and says sorry.
But I went back through our tracker tonight. It isn't just Eshaan. It's all of us, me included. Our estimates are off by two or three days almost every time. Nobody is being lazy. Everyone imagines the smooth version: no bugs, no meetings, no sick days.
Tomorrow at stand-up I'll try something new. Instead of "When will it be done?" I'll ask, "What's the earliest, and what's the realistic date?" And I'll show everyone our old estimates next to reality. Not to shame. Just so we can see it.
Omkar

qa.q: How many times in a month has Eshaan promised a Monday?
qa.a: Third time in a month.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling at first about Eshaan's promise?
qa.a: Omkar felt angry, being the one who has to call the client and apologise.

qa.q: What does Omkar plan to change at stand-up, and why?
qa.a: To ask for the earliest and the realistic date and show old estimates next to reality, so the team sees the pattern without being shamed.

qa.q: How might Eshaan react to seeing everyone's old estimates on screen?
qa.a: Eshaan might feel relieved that it isn't only him, and more willing to give honest ranges.

grounding: A lead's diary shows noticing a teammate's repeatedly optimistic dates, finding the whole team does it, and asking for ranges instead of blame.

passage: Bhavna's phone was full of them: the girl from Nagpur who left school at fifteen and now had two million followers, the boy who failed Class 12 and built a sneaker brand. Every video ended the same way: "School is a waste. Just start." One evening in their Andheri flat Bhavna told her elder sister Sarika she wanted to drop out after Class 10 and make videos full time. "Look how easy it is. They all made it." Sarika put down her laptop. "How many people do you think tried the same thing?" Bhavna shrugged. "I don't know. These people did it." "The ones who didn't make it don't make videos about it," Sarika said. "You're only seeing the winners. Where are the thousands who quit and are stuck?" Bhavna opened her mouth, then scrolled her feed again, slower this time.

qa.q: What did every video on Bhavna's phone end with?
qa.a: School is a waste. Just start.

qa.q: Why did dropping out seem so easy to Bhavna?
qa.a: She felt excited and inspired because every video she saw showed someone who had made it, so success seemed normal and certain.

qa.q: What question could Bhavna ask whenever she sees a success story?
qa.a: How many people tried the same thing and didn't make it, since the ones who failed rarely post videos.

qa.q: How does Sarika see the videos Bhavna shows her?
qa.a: Sarika sees them as a small, visible slice of winners, hiding the many who quit and are stuck.

grounding: Shows a teenager seeing only dropouts who succeeded and concluding the path is easy, until her sister asks about those who failed.

passage: The summer I turned sixteen, I was sure I'd skip college and become a playback singer. I'm Jahnavi, and my phone was full of reality-show winners from small towns, all saying, "I followed my dream, and look at me now." It looked simple: audition, get noticed, sing for films. My Rekha Mami was the one who stopped me, gently. She'd auditioned for four shows in her twenties. "Do you know how many girls were in my queue in Hyderabad?" she asked. "Three thousand. Two got through. The rest of us went home and nobody filmed us." I hadn't thought about the queue at all. Only the winners were on my screen. I still sing, and I still audition. But I also enrolled in college, and I stopped thinking the path was easy.

qa.q: How many girls were in Rekha Mami's audition queue in Hyderabad?
qa.a: Three thousand, and two got through.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling that summer about becoming a singer?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt certain and excited, because the winners on the screen made the path look simple.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi change after the talk with Rekha Mami, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Jahnavi kept singing and auditioning but also enrolled in college, keeping the dream while seeing how many never make it.

qa.q: What was the audition like for the people who went home?
qa.a: For the thousands who didn't get through, it probably meant quiet disappointment, with nobody filming or telling their stories.

passage:
Mentor's note, first-year entrepreneurship cell, 14 October.
Hansa came to our session today with a new routine copied from a famous founder: waking at 4 a.m., cold showers, no social life, skipping lectures to "build." She has stopped attending her statistics class. When I asked why, she showed me three interviews with billionaires who do the same. "It worked for them," she said.
Vidya, sitting next to her, asked the question I was going to ask: "How many people wake at four and skip class and don't become billionaires?" Hansa laughed, but then she went quiet.
I suggested she look up a list of failed start-ups from our own city and count what their founders did. Next session, I'll ask her what she found. I also asked her to go to Thursday's statistics class.

qa.q: What time does Hansa's copied routine have her wake up?
qa.a: At 4 a.m.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she went quiet after Vidya's question?
qa.a: She seemed unsettled and doubtful, realising she had only seen the founders who succeeded with those habits.

qa.q: What did the mentor suggest, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Looking up failed start-ups from their city and counting what their founders did, to see the whole group and not only winners.

qa.q: Why might Vidya see the famous founders differently from Hansa?
qa.a: Vidya thinks about the many people with the same habits who never succeeded, while Hansa sees only the few who did.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a student copying famous founders' habits without seeing how many with the same habits failed.

passage:
Monday. The bootcamp's website was full of smiling alumni: "From teacher to software engineer in 12 weeks!" Pema was tempted. Jomon, her flatmate, had already signed up. "Look at them all," he said.
Wednesday. Before paying, Pema emailed the bootcamp: "How many people started your last three batches, how many finished, and how many got developer jobs within six months?" She also found a forum of past students.
The following Tuesday. The bootcamp sent a vague reply about "many success stories." The forum was clearer: out of one batch of ninety, about thirty finished, and around fifteen got developer jobs. Several said they'd been left in debt. Pema didn't sign up. She looked for a cheaper evening course with published numbers, and asked Jomon, gently, if he had seen the forum.

qa.q: How many people from the batch of ninety got developer jobs, according to the forum?
qa.a: Around fifteen got developer jobs.

qa.q: Why did Pema email the bootcamp before paying?
qa.a: She felt tempted but cautious, wanting to know about everyone who started, not only the smiling alumni on the website.

qa.q: What would you advise someone choosing a course with glowing success stories?
qa.a: Ask, as Pema did, how many started, how many finished and how many reached the promised result, and look for past students' own accounts.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when Pema asks if he has seen the forum?
qa.a: Jomon might feel uneasy or defensive, having already signed up based on the alumni photos alone.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful person asking where the dropouts and failures are before trusting a course's success stories.

passage: Damini, you're asking whether to follow that fitness trainer everyone's praising? Let your Aditi Mausi tell you about my first job, at an ad agency in Mumbai. Our boss came back from a conference with a new method. "All the top agencies use it," he said, showing us three famous campaigns. Everyone clapped. I was twenty-four and I wanted to clap too. Instead I asked, in a very small voice, "Which agencies tried it and didn't do well?" The room went quiet. He didn't know. So I spent a weekend calling people I knew at other firms. Four had tried it. Three had dropped it within a year; it cost too much time. Only the successes had made it to the conference. We tried a small version on one client instead. The boss never thanked me. But we didn't lose a year.

qa.q: How many of the four firms Aditi called had dropped the method within a year?
qa.a: Three had dropped it within a year.

qa.q: What was young Aditi feeling when she asked her question in the meeting?
qa.a: She felt nervous, asking in a very small voice, because everyone else was clapping.

qa.q: Which choice in the story saved the agency a year?
qa.a: Calling other firms to find out who had tried the method and failed, then trying only a small version on one client.

qa.q: How might the boss have felt when the room went quiet?
qa.a: The boss was probably embarrassed and a little irritated, having shown only the famous successes without knowing about the failures.

grounding: An elder recalls asking which firms had failed with a method before praising it, and finding that only the successes were visible.

passage: The vendor needed an answer by five. Their sales rep had shown Mohit, the new operations manager at the logistics firm, a slide of glowing case studies: seven companies that had cut delivery times using the new routing software. Mohit's boss had already said, "Looks good, sign it." It was 3:30 and the warehouse was noisy with the evening shift. Urmila, from finance, leaned over. "Seven is a lot." "Seven out of how many?" Mohit said. He called the rep. "How many clients do you have in total, and how many cancelled in the first year?" A long pause. "We have about sixty. Around twenty didn't renew." Mohit asked for two names from the twenty. At 4:45 he called one of them: the software hadn't worked with their older scanners, like his. He wrote to his boss: "Let's test it at one warehouse first."

qa.q: How many clients did the vendor have in total?
qa.a: About sixty, and around twenty didn't renew.

qa.q: What might Mohit have been feeling when his boss said "sign it"?
qa.a: He was likely uneasy and cautious, feeling pressure to agree but doubting that seven glowing case studies told the whole story.

qa.q: What did Mohit do that helped under time pressure?
qa.a: He asked how many clients had cancelled, called one of them, and proposed a one-warehouse test instead of signing straight away.

qa.q: How might Urmila see the case-study slide at first?
qa.a: Urmila was impressed by seven successes, seeing them as a lot before anyone asked how many others had failed.

grounding: Shows a manager under time pressure asking where the failures are before trusting a vendor's success stories.

passage: My grandfather likes to walk me past the old stone buildings near the fort in Jodhpur. "See? They built things to last back then. Now everything cracks in ten years," he says. I'm Ujjwal, and I'm an architect, so you'd think I'd argue. For a long time I didn't, because he seemed right. Then one afternoon, digging through the city archives for a project with my colleague Arohi, I found old survey maps from 1910. Hundreds of buildings were marked where there's nothing now. Mud-brick houses, cheap shops, badly built havelis. They fell down decades ago. The stone ones we see today are the survivors, the best of their time. The bad ones simply aren't there to compare. I still love walking with Dadaji. But now when he says "back then," I think about the maps.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal find in the city archives?
qa.a: Old survey maps from 1910, with hundreds of buildings marked where there's nothing now.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling on seeing the old maps?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt surprised and thoughtful, seeing that the old buildings still standing are only the survivors, not proof that everything was better built.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal say to Dadaji to share this gently?
qa.a: Ujjwal could show him the 1910 maps and ask what happened to all the buildings that are gone, without dismissing his love for the old ones.

qa.q: How does Dadaji see the old stone buildings?
qa.a: Dadaji sees them as proof that people built to last back then, because the weaker buildings are no longer there to compare.

grounding: A young architect notices that only the durable old buildings survive, so 'old is better' talk misses the weak ones that are gone.

passage:
Site note, heritage survey, old market, Kolkata. Week 3.
The caretaker, Ganga-di, told me again today, "They don't make buildings like this now." She means the arcade with the iron columns, and she's proud of it. It is beautiful. But I checked the municipal records this week. In 1930 this market had five arcades. Four were timber and brick, cheaply built, and burned or collapsed by the 1960s. Only this one, the most expensive, survived. So of course the survivor is well made. The weak ones aren't here to remind anyone.
I didn't argue with her. I asked if she remembered the other arcades. She did, one of them, a fire when she was small. She was quiet after that.
Next step: add a panel about the lost arcades to our report, so visitors see the whole picture.
Kiran

qa.q: How many arcades did the market have in 1930?
qa.a: Five arcades.

qa.q: How does Kiran seem to feel about Ganga-di's pride in the arcade?
qa.a: Kiran seems respectful and gentle, admiring the arcade too but uneasy about the claim, so Kiran asks a question instead of arguing.

qa.q: What is Kiran's next step, and why does it help?
qa.a: Adding a panel about the lost arcades to the report, so visitors see that the surviving arcade is not the whole picture.

qa.q: How might Ganga-di see the iron arcade after the conversation?
qa.a: She may still be proud of it, but, quiet and a little sad after remembering the fire, also see it as the lucky survivor among weaker buildings that were lost.

grounding: A young surveyor's note observes that old buildings seem better made because only the durable ones remain, while weaker ones have vanished.

passage:
Thursday.
Ramesh uncle came for dinner and did his usual speech. "Songs from the seventies were real music. Today's songs are rubbish." Papa nodded. I nodded too, to keep the peace.
But on the drive home I kept thinking. Ramesh uncle remembers maybe forty great songs from the seventies. The radio still plays them, so we all know them. What about the thousands of forgettable songs from then? They didn't survive. Nobody plays them, so nobody remembers they existed. Of course the old songs we hear sound better. We're hearing the best of ten years, and comparing it to everything from this one week.
I'm not going to lecture Ramesh uncle. But next time, I might ask him to name ten bad songs from 1975. I bet he can't.
Nirmal

qa.a: Maybe forty great songs from the seventies.

qa.q: What was Nirmal feeling while nodding at dinner?
qa.a: Nirmal felt a bit uneasy, agreeing only to keep the peace while doubting that old songs were really better.

qa.a: Nirmal plans to ask Ramesh uncle to name ten bad songs from 1975, which gently shows that the forgettable ones have disappeared.

passage: The bus to school was late, it was pouring, and Dhruv had exactly one minute at the stationery shop before it came. Every boy in Class 4 had the same thing now: a spinning top with flashing lights. Dhruv didn't even like tops. He liked drawing comics with his sister Devika's old pens. But yesterday at lunch, the whole table had been spinning theirs, and he'd been the only one with nothing, just watching. "One spinning top," he said to the shopkeeper, pushing his saved money across the counter, rain dripping from his hair. "The blue one. No, the red. Whichever everyone has." At lunch he spun it. Everyone cheered. That night he put it in a drawer and went back to his comic, feeling uneasy.

qa.q: What did every boy in Class 4 have now?
qa.a: A spinning top with flashing lights.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv buy the top even though he didn't like tops?
qa.a: He felt left out watching the whole table spin theirs, and being included mattered more to him than what he actually enjoyed.

qa.q: What could Dhruv try next time everyone has something new?
qa.a: He could ask himself whether he really likes it, and maybe share his comics at lunch, so he can belong without changing his taste.

qa.q: How might Devika see Dhruv's new top?
qa.a: Devika might be surprised, since she knows he prefers drawing comics with her old pens.

grounding: Shows a child in a rush buying the toy everyone has, changing his taste to fit in though he prefers drawing.

passage: In the Sector 21 park in Chandigarh, all the boys had started collecting cricket cards. Amandeep used to love collecting leaves and pressing them in his big atlas. On Monday he told his mother Kavitha he wanted cards too. "I thought you didn't like cricket," she said. "Everybody has them," Amandeep said. "Everybody." By Wednesday he had spent his pocket money on three packs. He traded and learned words like "rare" and "shiny." But at home he didn't open the cards. He sat on the balcony and pressed a neem leaf into the atlas. At dinner she asked, "Do you like the cards?" He took a long time to answer. "I like being in the group." "And the leaves?" He smiled a little. "I like the leaves."

qa.a: Three packs of cricket cards.

qa.q: How could Kavitha support Amandeep?
qa.a: She could help him find a way to belong without giving up what he loves, maybe by inviting a friend to press leaves or trading only a few cards.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Amandeep's sudden interest in cards?
qa.a: Kavitha seems gently doubtful, knowing he didn't like cricket, so she watches and asks rather than scolding.

grounding: Shows a child switching from pressing leaves to collecting cricket cards because everyone has them and belonging matters more than taste.
